summary: Describes how the DEFLATE compression algorithm is used inside the IP Payload Compression Protocol. It fills in the details of what the compressed payload looks like when DEFLATE is the chosen method. It is informational and does not define an Internet standard.

eli5.summary: DEFLATE is a way of packing data tightly, like the trick that makes a zip file small. This note says how to use that trick on the pieces of data traveling through the internet.

questions: how is deflate used with ipcomp
what is ip payload compression using deflate
what is the minimum size to compress in ipcomp
subtitle: How the DEFLATE compression algorithm plugs into the IP Payload Compression Protocol.

tldr.problem: The IP Payload Compression Protocol (IPComp) can compress IP datagrams with different algorithms, but each algorithm needs its own definition of how it is used.
tldr.mechanism: This memo defines DEFLATE as an IPComp algorithm: everything after the IPComp header is DEFLATE-compressed, history is cleared between packets, and buffers under 90 bytes are not compressed.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational companion to the IPComp specification, RFC 2393, and has to be read together with it.

today: RFC 2394 is an Informational memo from December 1998 and, according to the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It is a companion to RFC 2393.

sections.title: Introduction and Why DEFLATE
sections.content:
IPComp allows the compression of IP datagrams using a choice of compression algorithms. This document describes how to integrate the DEFLATE algorithm into IPComp. It SHOULD be read in conjunction with the IPComp specification, RFC 2393, and MUST be taken in its context.

The memo lists the features of DEFLATE: it is used by PKZIP and gzip and embodied in the freely distributed zlib library, it has an open specification, and it has a low-overhead escape mechanism for incompressible data. It has been heavily used for many years on modem and other point-to-point links, and easily achieves 2:1 compression on the Calgary corpus using less than 64KBytes of memory on both sender and receiver. The DEFLATE specification itself is RFC 1951.
sections.eli5: IP packets can be squeezed to save space, and there are several ways to squeeze. This note picks the same squeezing trick that zip files use.

sections.title: Compressing and Decompressing
sections.content:
Compression follows the IP Compression Association (IPCA), which MUST define DEFLATE as the algorithm. The data from the IP datagram is compressed and placed after the IPComp header. For a TCP datagram, IP TCP ... becomes IP IPCOMP (TCP ...), with everything after the IPComp header compressed.

Because IPComp is stateless, DEFLATE history MUST be cleared between packets, both when compressing and when decompressing. DEFLATE offers several compression levels from best-but-slow to fast. The level used is implementation dependent, since any level is compatible with the decompressor.

On receipt, the data after the IPComp header is decompressed following RFC 1951 and replaces the IPComp header within the IP packet.
sections.eli5: The sender squeezes everything after a small label and the receiver unsqueezes it. Each packet is squeezed on its own, so nobody has to remember the earlier packets.

sections.title: Size Threshold
sections.content:
Compressing small buffers usually does not pay off, because the time to compress can exceed the time to transport the data. Informal tests show that the average buffer size that produces a larger result is around 90 bytes, so implementations SHOULD NOT attempt to compress buffers smaller than 90 bytes.

Apart from this packet size limit, the memo defines no compressibility test.
sections.eli5: Squeezing a tiny note takes more effort than it saves, so notes under 90 bytes are just sent as they are.

sections.title: Transform Identifier and Security
sections.content:
The IPsec Domain of Interpretation (RFC 2407) states that the ISAKMP IPCOMP transform ID for this algorithm is IPCOMP_DEFLATE. No other ISAKMP parameters are required.

The security considerations section says only that this document adds nothing beyond what the IPComp specification and the DEFLATE specification already declare.
sections.eli5: The algorithm has a name tag, IPCOMP_DEFLATE, so two computers can agree to use it. It adds no new safety worries of its own.
